blurb: Neurons, loss, gradient descent and backpropagation — the engine underneath every model.

lessons.title: A neuron is a weighted vote

cards.title: From one neuron to a network

steps.p: A neuron multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the total through a simple nonlinear function.
Each layer's outputs become the next layer's inputs. Early layers detect simple patterns; later ones combine them into abstract features.
Without it, any stack of layers collapses into one linear map — no more expressive than a single layer.

cards.aside: "Learning" just means finding weight values that make the network's outputs useful.

cards.statement: Stacking ten linear layers with no activation functions gives a more powerful model than one linear layer.
cards.why: False. Composing linear maps gives another linear map: W₃(W₂(W₁x)) = Wx. Depth only adds power when nonlinearities sit between the layers.

cards.q: ReLU (max(0, x)) largely replaced the sigmoid in deep networks mainly because…
options: Its gradient doesn't shrink toward zero for positive inputs
cards.why: Healthy gradients. A sigmoid flattens at both ends, so gradients through many layers shrink. ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs, letting signal flow through deep stacks. It is also cheap to compute.

cards.q: The universal approximation theorem says a network with one wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. What does it NOT promise?
options: That gradient descent will find them, or that the layer is a practical size
That it works for any input
cards.why: Existence, not learnability. The theorem says suitable weights exist, possibly with an enormous number of neurons. It says nothing about finding them efficiently — which is why depth matters in practice.

cards.title: A 1969 book proving simple perceptrons couldn't learn XOR helped trigger the first AI winter.
cards.detail: Minsky and Papert's "Perceptrons" showed single-layer networks cannot represent functions like exclusive-or. Multi-layer networks can, but nobody had a good way to train them until backpropagation spread in the 1980s.

cards.statement: A single-layer perceptron can learn to compute XOR.
cards.why: False. XOR's true cases (0,1) and (1,0) cannot be separated from (0,0) and (1,1) by one straight line. A single hidden layer fixes it.

cards.title: Walking downhill in a million dimensions

steps.p: A loss function scores how bad the predictions are. For language models it is cross-entropy: how surprised the model was by the real next token.
The gradient says how the loss changes as each weight changes. Stepping against it lowers the loss.

steps.h: Take small steps on small batches
steps.p: Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a mini-batch of examples and takes a step scaled by the learning rate. Repeat millions of times.

cards.aside: The loss landscape of a large model has billions of dimensions, yet this simple procedure works remarkably well.

cards.q: What typically happens if the learning rate is set far too high?
options: The loss oscillates or explodes instead of decreasing
cards.why: Divergence. Steps overshoot the valley floor and land higher up the other side, growing each time. Too low a rate is the opposite problem: stable but painfully slow.

cards.q: A model gives the correct next token a probability of 0.5. Its cross-entropy loss for that token, in nats, is about…
cards.why: ln 2 ≈ 0.69. Cross-entropy is −ln(p) for the true token. p = 1 gives 0 loss; p = 0.01 gives 4.6. Being confidently wrong is punished hard.

cards.statement: Stochastic gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire dataset before each update.
cards.why: False. That is full-batch gradient descent. SGD uses a small random batch, which is cheaper per step and adds noise that can actually help escape poor regions.

cards.title: The Adam optimizer stores two extra numbers for every parameter.
cards.detail: It tracks a running average of each weight's gradient and of its squared gradient. With FP32 copies, optimizer state alone can need several times more memory than the BF16 model weights.

cards.q: Perplexity is e raised to the loss. A model with a perplexity of 10 is roughly as uncertain as…
options: Choosing uniformly among 10 equally likely tokens
cards.why: A fair 10-sided die. Perplexity is the effective number of choices the model is hesitating between. Lower is better; a perfect model has perplexity 1.

cards.title: Blame, passed backwards

steps.p: Inputs flow through the network to a prediction and a loss. Intermediate activations are saved along the way.
Starting at the loss, the chain rule computes how much each layer's output contributed, then each layer's weights, moving from the last layer to the first.
One backward pass yields the gradient for all parameters at about twice the cost of the forward pass.

cards.aside: Frameworks like PyTorch do this automatically (autograd): you write the forward pass, and gradients come for free.

cards.q: Training compute is roughly 6 × parameters × tokens. About how many FLOPs to train a 7B model on 1 trillion tokens?
cards.why: 6 × 7×10⁹ × 10¹² = 4.2 × 10²². The 6 is ~2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward, plus ~4 backward. This one formula lets you size almost any training run.

cards.statement: Backpropagation needs the activations from the forward pass to be kept in memory.
cards.why: True. Each layer's gradient depends on its inputs. For large models that memory is a bottleneck, so "activation checkpointing" saves only some activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass.

cards.q: What is the largest slope a sigmoid function ever has?
cards.why: 0.25, at x = 0. Backprop multiplies one such factor per layer, so 10 sigmoid layers shrink gradients by at least 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶. That is the vanishing-gradient problem in one number.

cards.title: Backpropagation was popularized by a 1986 Nature paper — but invented earlier, more than once.
cards.detail: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams made it famous. Seppo Linnainmaa described reverse-mode automatic differentiation in 1970, and Paul Werbos proposed applying it to neural networks in 1974.

cards.statement: In PyTorch, you must write the gradient formula for each layer you create.
cards.why: False. Autograd records the operations you perform and applies the chain rule automatically when you call .backward(). Custom gradients are possible but rarely needed.

cards.title: Generalization

steps.p: Data is split into training, validation and test sets. Only the training set updates weights; the others measure how well the model handles unseen examples.
A model that keeps improving on training data while getting worse on validation data is memorizing quirks instead of learning patterns.
More data, dropout, weight decay and early stopping all push the model toward simpler explanations that transfer.

cards.aside: Large language models rarely overfit in the classic sense; most see each token only once or a few times.

options: Randomly zeroing a fraction of activations during training
cards.why: Random silencing. Each step, a random subset of units is switched off, so no unit can rely on specific partners. At inference all units are used, like averaging many thinned networks.

cards.statement: It is fine to tune hyperparameters by checking results on the test set.
cards.why: False. Every choice made by looking at the test set leaks it into training, making the final score optimistic. Tune on validation; touch the test set once at the end.

cards.q: Why do transformers use LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm?
options: It normalizes each token on its own, independent of batch size and sequence length
cards.why: Batch independence. BatchNorm relies on statistics across a batch, which is awkward for variable-length sequences and breaks at batch size 1. LayerNorm normalizes across features within each token.

cards.title: Some networks suddenly generalize long after they've perfectly memorized their training data — "grokking".
cards.detail: Power et al. (2022) trained small transformers on modular arithmetic. Validation accuracy stayed near chance for thousands of steps after training accuracy hit 100%, then jumped to near-perfect.

cards.q: A model with high variance (in the bias–variance sense) is one that…
options: Is too simple to fit the data
Fits noise in its particular training set and changes a lot with different samples
cards.why: Overfitting. High variance means predictions swing with the specific training sample. High bias is the opposite: a model too rigid to capture the real pattern.
